Workout Rest Was due
Turn pieces so matching inks touch: 6 joined hexes dissolve. Picture each turn in your mind first.
How to play it so it helps
  1. Soon after. Best within about 6 hours of the upsetting moment. Later can still help if you do step 2.
  2. A quick reminder first. Bring the moment to mind for a few seconds, like glancing at a photo. Don't replay it.
  3. Then play 10 to 20 minutes in one go. The ring counts it for you.
  4. Turn pieces in your head first. Picture where each piece fits and rotate it in your mind before you move it. That mental picturing is the part that works.
    Example: a cup-shaped piece appears. Don't touch anything yet. Find the spot you want, say a single bump on the left. Now turn the cup in your head, once, twice, until its opening sits over that bump. Only then make the moves to match the picture. If it lands where you imagined, you did it right.
  5. Keep it quiet. No other screens, chatting, or music with words while you play.
  6. If the memory pops up later, notice it, let it pass, and play another round if you want.
Why it works Right after something upsetting, your brain spends a few hours "saving" the memory, mostly as vivid pictures. A visual puzzle keeps that same part of your brain busy, so the memory is stored less vividly and pops back into your head less often. You still remember what happened; it just intrudes less. Tested in studies with people after accidents and traumatic events (Holmes et al., 2009; Iyadurai et al., 2018). Honeycomb's hexagons turn six ways, so they ask for a lot of mental rotation, which is the part that helps.

A gentle two-minute reset, wherever you are.

Gently shake out your hands, arms, jaw and legs. Let the tension fall away.

Splash cool water on your face, or hold a cold wet cloth to it for 30 seconds. It helps your heart slow down.
